stem: A 10-day-old girl who has been breastfed develops vomiting, jaundice and an enlarged liver. Her urine tests positive for reducing substances but negative on the glucose oxidase strip. Red-cell galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase activity is very low.
oneliner: 10-day-old girl + breastfed + vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly + urine reducing substance positive, glucose oxidase negative + low red-cell GALT → next dietary step?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate dietary step?

options.A: Continue breastfeeding and add oral glucose to the diet
options.B: Switch to a soy-based lactose-free formula
options.C: Strict dietary restriction of fructose and of sucrose
options.D: Strict dietary restriction of phenylalanine intake
options.E: High-protein diet supplemented with daily nicotinic acid

whyNot.A: **Breast milk contains lactose**, the galactose source; added glucose does not stop galactose-1-phosphate build-up
whyNot.C: Fructose restriction treats **hereditary fructose intolerance**; here **red-cell GALT is low**
whyNot.D: Phenylalanine restriction treats **PKU**, which does not cause **jaundice, hepatomegaly or low GALT**
whyNot.E: That is the **Hartnup** treatment; it does nothing for **galactose** metabolism

answer: Switch to a soy-based lactose-free formula
why: Low **GALT** with **reducing substances in urine but a negative glucose oxidase test** is classic **galactosemia**. All **lactose and galactose** must be removed at once, so milk (breast or cow) is replaced with a **soy-based formula**; this prevents liver damage, cataracts and sepsis.

idea.rule: In galactosemia, remove lactose and galactose from the diet completely and immediately.
also: PKU: low-phenylalanine diet, tyrosine becomes essential
Hereditary fructose intolerance: avoid fructose, sucrose and sorbitol
MSUD: restrict leucine, isoleucine and valine
Glycogen storage disease I: frequent feeds and cornstarch

stem: A 4-month-old boy has marked hypotonia, a large tongue, trouble feeding and an enlarged heart on chest x-ray. Glucose, lactate and uric acid are normal. A muscle biopsy shows lysosomes packed with glycogen.
oneliner: 4-month-old boy + floppy + macroglossia + feeding difficulty + cardiomegaly + normal glucose, lactate, uric acid + lysosomal glycogen in muscle → treatment?
ask: Which of the following is the best treatment?

options.C: Strict restriction of galactose and fructose in feeds

whyNot.B: Cornstarch treats **hypoglycemia in glycogen storage disease I**; this baby has **normal glucose and lactate**
whyNot.C: Treats **galactosemia and fructose intolerance**; they do not cause **cardiomegaly with lysosomal glycogen**
whyNot.D: Glucagon helps **fasting hypoglycemia**; here glucose is **normal** and the defect is lysosomal
whyNot.E: Used for some **other lysosomal diseases** (e.g. Hurler), not the standard treatment for this glycogenosis

why: Lysosomal glycogen with cardiomegaly and a floppy infant is **Pompe disease** (**acid alpha-glucosidase** deficiency). Treatment is **enzyme replacement** with recombinant **acid alpha-glucosidase (alglucosidase alfa)**, which improves heart and muscle disease.

idea.rule: Lysosomal storage diseases with a missing enzyme are treated by replacing that enzyme.
also: Gaucher disease: imiglucerase (glucocerebrosidase)
Fabry disease: agalsidase
Hurler syndrome: laronidase plus transplant
Hunter syndrome: idursulfase (iduronate-2-sulfatase)

stem: A 22-year-old woman with mild intellectual disability has a downward-dislocated lens and a long-limbed, tall frame. She presents with acute femoral artery thrombosis. Plasma homocysteine and methionine are both markedly elevated.
oneliner: 22F + mild intellectual disability + downward lens dislocation + tall and long-limbed + femoral artery thrombosis + high homocysteine and methionine → treatment?
ask: Which of the following is the best treatment?

options.A: Restrict cysteine intake and supplement methionine instead
options.B: Restrict branched-chain amino acids in the diet
options.C: Restrict phenylalanine intake and add tyrosine
options.D: Start a beta-blocker and losartan to protect the aorta
options.E: Pyridoxine, low-methionine diet and added cysteine

whyNot.A: That is **backwards**: methionine is already high and **cysteine becomes essential**
whyNot.B: Treats **MSUD** (sweet urine, ketoacidosis); this woman has **high methionine and homocysteine**
whyNot.C: Treats **PKU** (mousy odor, hypopigmentation); she has **lens dislocation and thrombosis**
whyNot.D: Used for **Marfan syndrome**; her lens is displaced **downward** with **high homocysteine**, so the aorta is not the target

answer: Pyridoxine, low-methionine diet and added cysteine
why: High **homocysteine and methionine** with **downward ectopia lentis** and thrombosis is **cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency**. Treatment is **pyridoxine (B6)**, with **folate and B12**, a **methionine-restricted diet** and **cysteine supplementation**, since cysteine can no longer be made.

idea.rule: In CBS deficiency, cysteine becomes essential and methionine must be limited; B6 is the cofactor that may rescue the enzyme.
also: PKU: tyrosine becomes essential
MSUD: restrict leucine, isoleucine and valine
Marfan: ectopia lentis is upward, no thrombosis
Betaine, folate and B12 also lower homocysteine by remethylation

stem: A 5-day-old boy is lethargic and feeding poorly, with alternating floppy and stiff posture. His urine smells sweet, like burnt sugar. Plasma branched-chain amino acids and alloisoleucine are markedly raised, and he has ketoacidosis.
oneliner: 5-day-old boy + lethargy and poor feeding + alternating hypotonia and hypertonia + sweet burnt-sugar urine + raised branched-chain amino acids and alloisoleucine + ketoacidosis → dietary restriction?
ask: Which dietary restriction is the cornerstone of treatment?

options.D: Restrict galactose and lactose from all feeds
options.E: Restrict fructose and sucrose in the diet

whyNot.A: Treats **PKU** (musty odor); this urine smells **sweet, like burnt sugar**
whyNot.B: Treats **homocystinuria** (ectopia lentis, thrombosis); here the **branched-chain amino acids** are high
whyNot.D: Treats **galactosemia** (jaundice, cataracts, E. coli sepsis); it does not explain **sweet-smelling urine and raised branched-chain amino acids**
whyNot.E: Treats **hereditary fructose intolerance** (vomiting after fruit and sugar, hypoglycemia); it does not raise **branched-chain amino acids**

why: Sweet urine with high **leucine, isoleucine and valine** is **maple syrup urine disease**: a **branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase** defect. Treatment is a diet **restricting branched-chain amino acids**, with **thiamine** (a cofactor) tried in some patients.

idea.rule: Restrict the amino acids that pile up behind the block.
also: PKU: restrict phenylalanine
Homocystinuria: restrict methionine
Tyrosinemia: restrict phenylalanine and tyrosine
Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase needs thiamine, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD and NAD

stem: A 14-year-old girl with poor dietary intake has an itchy, sun-induced rash on her face and arms and unsteady gait. Urine amino acid screening shows excess neutral amino acids, and serum tryptophan is low.
oneliner: 14F + poor diet + sun-induced itchy rash + unsteady gait + neutral aminoaciduria + low serum tryptophan → treatment?
ask: Which of the following is the best treatment?

options.A: Low-protein diet with sodium benzoate supplementation
options.C: Strict dietary restriction of tryptophan intake only
options.D: Daily thiamine supplementation with a high-fat diet

whyNot.A: Used for **hyperammonemia / urea cycle defects**; this girl has a **photosensitive rash and neutral aminoaciduria**
whyNot.C: Her **tryptophan is already low**; restricting it would worsen the **niacin deficiency**
whyNot.D: Thiamine with a high-fat diet treats **pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency**, not a **sun-induced rash with neutral aminoaciduria**
whyNot.E: Chelates copper in **Wilson disease**; not relevant to **neutral aminoaciduria**

why: Neutral aminoaciduria with low tryptophan and a **pellagra-like rash** is **Hartnup disease** (defective neutral amino acid transporter). Treatment is a **high-protein diet and nicotinic acid (niacin)**, since tryptophan is the precursor for niacin.

idea.rule: Hartnup is pellagra from lost tryptophan, so feed protein and give niacin.
also: Pellagra: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia
Carcinoid syndrome diverts tryptophan to serotonin and can cause pellagra
Isoniazid blocks B6 and can cause pellagra-like disease
Corn-based diets (bound niacin, little tryptophan) also cause pellagra

stem: A newborn boy has a high phenylalanine level on screening, and the phenylalanine hydroxylase gene is normal. Over the next months, despite strict dietary phenylalanine restriction, he develops progressive neurologic decline. CSF dopamine and serotonin metabolites are low.
oneliner: Newborn boy + high phenylalanine on screen + normal PAH gene + decline despite low-Phe diet + low CSF dopamine and serotonin metabolites → treatment?
ask: Which of the following is the best treatment?

options.A: Stricter dietary phenylalanine restriction without any other change
options.B: Tyrosine supplementation while keeping the same low-phenylalanine diet
options.C: High-dose pyridoxine (vitamin B6) supplementation given alone
options.E: Biotin supplementation together with a low-protein diet

whyNot.A: His **phenylalanine is already controlled** by diet yet he worsens; **neurotransmitter synthesis** is still broken
whyNot.B: Tyrosine does not restore **dopamine and serotonin**; both need **BH4-dependent hydroxylases**
whyNot.C: B6 treats **homocystinuria** and some seizures; it does not replace **BH4**
whyNot.E: Biotin treats **carboxylase deficiency**; not a cause of **low CSF dopamine and serotonin**

why: A **normal PAH gene** with high phenylalanine and low CSF **dopamine and serotonin** points to **BH4 (tetrahydrobiopterin) deficiency**. BH4 is also the cofactor for **tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylase**, so the fix is **BH4 replacement plus L-dopa and 5-hydroxytryptophan**.

idea.rule: BH4 is the cofactor for phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylases, so a BH4 defect hits all three pathways.
also: Phenylalanine hydroxylase: Phe to tyrosine
Tyrosine hydroxylase: dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine pathway
Tryptophan hydroxylase: serotonin pathway
Nitric oxide synthase also uses BH4
